entities.name: William IV, Duke of Aquitaine
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
William IV, known as "Fierebras" (Iron-Arm), was the Duke of Aquitaine and Count of Poitou from 963 until his retirement to a monastery in 990, dying on February 8, 994. His reign unfolded during a critical period of post-Carolingian fragmentation in West Francia, where regional potentates like the Dukes of Aquitaine were consolidating power against both the nascent Capetian monarchy and ambitious neighboring counts. William IV's significance lies in his efforts to stabilize and assert ducal authority within his vast territories, navigating complex feudal loyalties and external pressures that would define the political landscape of medieval France.

Throughout his ducal tenure, William IV was embroiled in a series of conflicts, most notably with Geoffrey I "Grisegonelle" (Greymantle), Count of Anjou, over disputed territories such as Loudun and Mirebeau. These intermittent wars, often characterized by sieges and skirmishes, were crucial in defining the borders and influence of Aquitaine against its powerful eastern neighbor. Internally, William also faced challenges from rebellious vassals and even his own brother, Otto, necessitating a firm hand in governance. Beyond military endeavors, he was a patron of monasticism, supporting foundations like the Abbey of Saint-Cyprien of Poitiers and the Abbey of Maillezais, reflecting the era's blend of martial power and religious devotion.
